In a model of a river basin in northeast China, wetlands beside rivers eased drought and helped keep low flows going during the severe drought of 2011 [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2, ev_drought_hazard_wu23_6]. A review of African wetlands says they are essential dry-season grazing for wild and domestic animals, helping herds through severe dry seasons and droughts [ev_drought_hazard_fyn15_1]. An IUCN project report on the Waza Logone floodplain in Cameroon says the presence of floods helps reduce the impacts and severity of drought [ev_drought_hazard_loth04_7]. In a Canadian basin model, adding wetland area gradually made up for climate-driven falls in summer low flows [ev_wet_eff_goy22_2].
caveats: The class is low and no source gives a size. mitigation_mechanism: Rewetting drained peat moderately reduces fire. Drainage dries the peat and makes it burn; raising the water table back up keeps the fuel wet [ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1, ev_wgy_ram_14, ev_fire_hazard_page09_3]. Most of the evidence, and all of the sizes, come from tropical peat in Indonesia (with one Malaysian case). After large-scale canal blocking in Riau (Taufik et al.), the frequency of continuous extreme fire-hazard events fell by 40%, but the average area affected was only 5% lower than before rewetting [ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_1, ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_2]. In a matched comparison (Salmayenti et al.), peat restored with dams had significantly fewer fire hotspots in 2019 than similar unrestored peat, 5 against 6 per square km [ev_wet_eff_salm26_1]. A model of Indonesian peatland restoration (Tan et al.) puts the reduction in fire risk at 6%–37% [ev_fire_hazard_tan22_1], and a Malaysian community group that patrols, plants and blocks drains helped cut the extent of forest fires in its area by 98% between 2014 and 2022 [ev_fire_hazard_unepgpa22_3]. Fires are more frequent close to drainage canals, the effect reaching at least 800 m from them [ev_fire_hazard_jauhiainen16_5]. Global syntheses and guidance say the same thing without giving a size: rewetting wetlands reduces risk of peat fires (Griscom et al.), rewetting and restoration are efficient ways to reduce wildfire risk in drained peatlands (UNEP Global Peatlands Assessment), and fire on rewetted organic soils is considered low compared with drained soils (IPCC wetlands supplement) [ev_fire_hazard_griscom17_9, ev_fire_hazard_unepgpa22_1, ev_fire_hazard_ipcc13wl_2].
caveats: Rewetting does not stop fire in extreme drought years. In Riau, widespread prolonged extreme fire hazard occurred only in the drying El Niño years, the mean duration of extreme events rose after rewetting, and that duration was controlled by the weather, not by rewetting [ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_3, ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_4]. The matched comparison found no significant difference between restored and unrestored peat in 2023 [ev_wet_eff_salm26_3]; restoration at one high-priority Indonesian village has so far been largely ineffective in reducing fire risk [ev_wet_eff_mend24_1]; and almost 50% of one agro-sylvofishery project burned in the 2019 El Niño, which the authors link to trade-offs in the project design [ev_wet_fire_budi20_2], while a neighbouring revegetation project survived the large fires and held back fire spreading in from nearby [ev_wet_fire_budi20_1]. The Riau sizes come from satellite fire-hazard records treated as a model, the 6%–37% is modelled, and the Malaysian 98% is a bundled community programme reported by an assessment, not a measured effect of rewetting alone. Many statements are project claims or expert judgement with no fire data [ev_wet_fire_terz22_1, ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_1]. Settings are upper-middle-income Indonesia and Malaysia plus guidance from Europe and Canada; no low-income site is represented. The benefit is off-site for farmers: it lowers landscape fire and smoke rather than protecting a plot.

mitigation_mechanism: Rewetting moderately reduces fire. Raising the water table in drained peat, mainly by blocking canals, keeps the peat wet so it is harder to ignite. In a national comparison in Indonesia during the El Nino of 2019, peat restored with canal dams had fewer fire hotspots than matched unrestored peat (5 against 6 per square kilometre) [ev_wet_eff_salm26_1]. A modelled fire-hazard index in Riau showed continuous extreme hazard 40% less often after rewetting [ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_1], and a planning model put the fall in fire risk at 6%–37% [ev_fire_hazard_tan22_1]. In Malaysia, community patrols together with drain blocking helped cut the extent of forest fires by 98% [ev_fire_hazard_unepgpa22_3]. A review notes that undrained peat swamp forest stays moist and is at very low fire risk, while drained peat next to farmland carries the greatest risk [ev_fire_hazard_jauhiainen16_4]. A global review of natural climate solutions also lists a lower risk of peat fires as a benefit of rewetting, citing earlier work second-hand [ev_fire_hazard_griscom17_9].
caveats: The benefit is moderate and fades in the worst years. In the El Nino of 2023, restored and unrestored peat showed no significant difference [ev_wet_eff_salm26_3]. mitigation_mechanism: Wetland management moderately reduces flood impacts close to the works. Rewetting and re-roughening land slows storm water, so flood peaks just below the works are lower. On UK peat, peak flows fell 27% where bare peat was re-vegetated, 51% where gullies were also blocked, and 49% at a rewetted gully [ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N, ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow]. Ditch and drain blocking on Irish and Welsh bogs made stream flow less flashy [ev_flood_hazard_hold04_2, ev_flood_hazard_wils11db_4]. Reconnecting floodplains cut modelled peaks by about 8% to 12% in a base case, and a review puts the average flood-peak cut from river and floodplain measures at 30% [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2, ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1]. Setting levees back lowered flood levels on large rivers [ev_flood_hazard_knox22_1, ev_flood_hazard_serra22_1]. A Canadian basin model found restored wetland eased the rise in spring flood peaks expected with climate change [ev_wet_eff_goy22_1].
caveats: The benefit is moderate because it is local and does not hold up at catchment scale or in big floods. No effect was found across a whole 260 km2 UK catchment, drain blocking is notoriously hard to detect at basin scale, and in major floods the whole basin is saturated so wetlands make no difference [ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null, ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null, ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null]. Placement can reverse the effect: a moorland scheme raised downstream risk, restoring the wrong reach raised flooding upstream, and moving a project downstream turned a 14% peak cut into about a 1% increase [ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal, ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4, ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4]. Rougher floodplains can make local flooding deeper and wider, and rewetting can use up storage that floods would fill [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up, ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost]. Guidance notes that drained peat is no longer saturated, which itself lowers peaks, so rewetting does not always help [ev_wgy_ram_10]. Most evidence is from the UK and US, much of it modelled, with no measured low- or lower-middle-income result. The benefit arrives downstream, not on the farm.

mitigation_mechanism: Studies disagree on whether wetland management lowers or raises flooding for farmers. On the side of a reduction, wooded wetlands in particular increase flood storage, reduce flood peaks and increase peak travel time [ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland], and a Ramsar briefing note states that wetland protection and restoration buffer communities by reducing wave damage and floods [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2]. On the side of an increase, the same review reports that even where the dominant result is to increase water storage within the wetland, the overall result may still be an increase in flood peaks at the catchment scale [ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment], and that a change of vegetation from wet meadows to shrubs and trees can double the size and depth of the inundated area for the same size of flood [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up].
caveats: What separates the two sides is scale and position: the reductions are storage and roughness effects on the flood peak passing through or below the wetland [ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland, ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2], while the increases arise at catchment scale, where an on-site storage gain need not add up to a downstream benefit [ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment], and locally, where the roughness that slows the flood raises water level and flooded area on the re-vegetated floodplain itself [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up]. The influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at the basin scale [ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null]; and during major catastrophic floods the whole basin may be saturated, so the presence or absence of wetlands, or their management, has no effect [ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null]. None of the units is a measurement of a flood outcome in this scope: they are a single review pooling UK, US, Canadian, Irish and Zimbabwean settings and a global policy brief. Any benefit falls downstream or at landscape scale rather than on the farmer's plot, and a farmer whose floodplain is re-vegetated may see deeper, wider flooding locally.

mitigation_mechanism: Coastal wetlands (salt marshes, mangroves) reduce flood impact mainly by dissipating wave energy and attenuating storm surge before it reaches land: salt-marsh vegetation has been measured giving a significant reduction in wave height compared with unvegetated mudflat, and across a global set of field measurements, coastal habitats reduced wave heights by 35% to 71% on average, with salt marshes alone cutting wave height by about 72%. Croplands within 1 km of mangroves and tidal marshes have also been found to experience less surface-water presence and smaller crop-cover declines than more distant areas.
caveats: This benefit does not hold at every severity level: the same review found salt marshes dissipate storm surge less effectively during extreme storms than during moderate ones, man-made levees and dikes behind a marsh can limit its surge-attenuating effect, and one study found neither crop type nor the simple presence of coastal wetlands added much explanatory power once other factors were accounted for. Only 2 of the 8 units measuring a benefit actually state its size, which is why the class is capped at a moderate level even though the direction is consistent. For most farmers this is an off-site benefit: the wetland sits off their land, and the protection shows up downstream or at landscape scale, not on their own plot.

mitigation_mechanism: Reconnecting and rewetting floodplains gives storm water somewhere to spread outside the channel. Modelled peak flow fell by up to 37% along a reconnected reach [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_1]; hollow wetlands could store 72% of the runoff from a 2-year storm [ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage]; and embanking a floodplain raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% [ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment]. Removing or setting back levees lowered flood levels: by 0.66 m on average along a reach, 50 cm on the Elbe and 0.3 m on the Dutch Rhine [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_1, ev_flood_hazard_serra22_1, ev_flood_hazard_knox22_4]. A meta-analysis finds that on average wetlands reduce flood frequency and size [ev_flood_hazard_kad16_1]. In a Canadian basin model, restored wetland eased the rise in spring flood peaks [ev_wet_eff_goy22_1].
caveats: The class is low: the clear evidence is local and for moderate storms. In extreme floods and at large catchment scale there is little or no effect [ev_wetflA_dads_summary_extreme_null, ev_wetflA_dads_largecatchment_null]; the same hollow wetlands held 41% of a 100-year storm, and at a catchment outlet the modelled peak fell by only 0.65% to 1.1% [ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage, ev_flood_hazard_worl23_2, ev_flood_hazard_worl23_3]. Measured studies show smaller effects than models [ev_flood_hazard_kad16_2]. Position can reverse the effect: upstream wetland raised downstream risk in a Chinese basin, restoring some reaches worsened flooding upstream, and Zimbabwean headwater dambos were found to generate storm runoff [ev_flood_hazard_wu23_4, ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4, ev_wetflA_acre_dambo_reversal]. Rewetting can also use up storage space floods would need [ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost]. Much evidence is about existing wetlands: a modelled Indonesian comparison found intact peat flooded less (5%) than degraded peat (25%) in a very wet year [ev_flood_hazard_page09_5]. The corpus is mostly temperate and high-income, and the benefit is off the farm.

mitigation_mechanism: Drought can switch off the flood pulse a restored floodplain depends on. On a restored floodplain the hazard works by removing the flood the wetland depends on: in 2020, lack of snow cover and severe drought meant no spring flooding on the Pripyat floodplain, and migrating and nesting birds on the restored floodplain meadows declined strongly (ev_wgy_blr_6).
caveats: This is one observation in a project terminal evaluation from Belarus, an upper-middle-income temperate setting, and the practice is restoration and maintenance of open floodplain meadows by grazing and mowing, not rewetting of drained land; the indicator is the number of migrating and nesting birds, not a livelihood or a hydrological measure, and the evaluation gives no size for the decline. The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to flooding, as well as to fire, drought and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_21). It does not say whether the flooding came from rivers or from the raised water table of rewetting itself, and it concerns tropical peat-swamp replanting only. The Berbak figure is the only measured loss rate, reported second-hand from van Eijk et al. at a single national-park site [ev_climate_shock_doh18_1]. Together these are a reason to budget for replanting losses and replacement, not a measured rate of loss. The Sumatran case is a single site on a project its authors describe as never fully rewetted; the sentence is cut by a page break, so the number of damaged blockings is not recoverable. mitigation_mechanism: Storm surge and flooding damage coastal wetlands, but the damage is rated low. A review of storm impacts on coastal wetland heights (Cahoon) records that in 2002 Hurricane Lili created 257 ha of open water, 0.5-1.3 m deep, at West Cote Blanche, Louisiana, by moving the marsh root mat sideways [ev_climate_shock_cah06_2], and that Hurricane Andrew compacted a severely degraded marsh at Bayou Chitigue by 33 mm in spite of sediment being laid down [ev_climate_shock_cah06_3].
caveats: The condition of the wetland decides the damage. A healthy marsh nearby at Old Oyster Bayou was not compacted by Hurricane Andrew but gained height equal to the sediment laid down [ev_climate_shock_cah06_4], so a newly restored or degraded site, where the ground is weakest, is the case to plan for. All of this comes from one review of existing, established marsh on US coasts, a high-income setting, not from restored sites, which is why the rating is low and uncertain.

mitigation_mechanism: The vulnerable asset is the canal dam that holds the water table up. In December 2005, after an extreme rainfall event, both dams in the Kalampangan Canal were damaged by water seeping underneath and along the sides; they were repaired in March 2006 and were damaged again in August 2006 (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_7). During an extreme rainfall event in August 2007 a further dam was damaged in a flash flood, the canal water level rising by several metres in a short period (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_8). The rainfall is the trigger; the vulnerability is structural, since highly permeable tropical peat lets seepage pass beneath and alongside a dam, and the sunken canals intercept overland and interflow, raising canal discharges when the rain is extreme.
caveats: This is a single demonstration site in Indonesian tropical peat, recorded as a case study rather than measured across projects, and the repeat failure after repair is the most transferable part of it. It says nothing about damage to the wetland itself, about coastal or temperate wetland types, or about water-control structures of other designs. Read it as a design and maintenance risk for canal-blocking programmes in deep permeable peat — dam siting relative to the contour, seepage control, and a repair budget that assumes recurrence — rather than as a general sensitivity of wetland management to extreme rainfall. Provenance: humid-tropical, upper-middle-income, with no comparable record from any other peat region.
